tooltip.title: Classification by Level of Split
tooltip.markdown: The fundamental histopathologic branch point for diagnosing autoimmune bullous diseases is the location of the blister within or below the epidermis. This guides the entire diagnostic workup.

tooltip.title: Intraepidermal Blistering
tooltip.markdown: Blisters form due to loss of adhesion between keratinocytes (acantholysis). These blisters are typically flaccid and rupture easily, leaving erosions.

tooltip.title: Suprabasal Split
tooltip.markdown: Cleavage occurs just above the basal cell layer, leaving a "row of tombstones." Caused by autoantibodies against desmosomal proteins.

tooltip.title: Subcorneal or Granular Layer Split
tooltip.markdown: A very superficial split high in the epidermis. Blisters are extremely fragile.

tooltip.title: Subepidermal Blistering
tooltip.markdown: Blisters form due to detachment of the entire epidermis from the underlying dermis at the basement membrane zone. These blisters are typically tense and remain intact.

tooltip.title: Eosinophil-Rich Infiltrate
tooltip.markdown: The inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis is primarily composed of eosinophils.

tooltip.title: Neutrophil-Rich Infiltrate
tooltip.markdown: The inflammatory infiltrate in the dermis is primarily composed of neutrophils, often forming microabscesses in the dermal papillae.

tooltip.title: Paucicellular (Non-inflammatory)
tooltip.markdown: Blistering occurs with minimal to no associated inflammation. Often associated with scarring.
